newsitem.title: UK: New hope for Briton who wants dead husband's baby.
newsitem.headline: New hope for Briton who wants dead husband's baby.

text.p: A British woman who lost a court battle to be artifically inseminated with her dead husband's sperm may be allowed to be treated with it abroad, Junior Health Minister John Horam said on Wednesday.
He told the House of Commons (lower house of parliament) during a debate on the case that the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HFEA) planned to reconsider its decision.
"It did decide last Thursday to give further consideration to one particular aspect of the case, namely the question of whether the gametes (sperm) could be exported," Horam said.
The HFEA said in a statement it was seeking more information and expected to reach a decision before the end of the year.
"The Authority has discretion to consider any additional information with regard to export in this case. It has chosen to do so in light of the new information available," it said.
"The authority's solicitors have written to Mrs (Diane) Blood's solicitors inviting them to submit any further evidence which they may wish to be considered."
The HFEA had banned Blood, 30, from using her husband's sperm because he had not given his written consent before he died from meningitis in March 1995.
Judge Stephen Brown, president of London's High Court family division, upheld the decision in a ruling nearly two weeks ago.

The case sparked intense debate about the government's role in issues concerning assisted conception, particularly because it also prevented her from taking the sperm to the United States or Belgium where doctors had agreed to treat her.
The HFEA had argued it would be illegal under the 1990 Human Fertilization and Embryology Act to allow the procedure in Britain or abroad without the husband's written consent.
Blood described the HFEA's latest decision as "good news."
"The fact that they've asked for it (more information) suggests to me that they want to look at the individual and very unique circumstances of my case," she told a news conference.
"And given that 90 percent of the population seems to support my case, I am hopeful."

Blood, who married in 1991, said she and her husband had been trying to have a baby for a year before he died. She also said she had the support of both her parents and her husband's parents in her quest to have his baby.
A leading British feritility expert, Dr Robert Forman, said the decision to ban the artificial insemination was based on rules and compassion had gone out the window.
